_readme: CADENCE KNOWLEDGE CONTRIBUTION TEMPLATE
Cadence is Acme's sales agent platform. Its brain is a vault of markdown that Owl,
the assistant, reads before it answers. This file is how knowledge from outside gets in.
HOW TO FILL IT IN
1. Copy this file and replace `contributed_by` with your name.
2. Replace the four worked examples in `entries` with your own. Keep the shape.
3. Send the file back. It gets imported into a review queue and approved by hand
before Owl can see any of it.
IF YOU ARE ASKING CLAUDE TO FILL THIS IN FOR YOU, paste this whole file and say:
'Fill in the `entries` array with what you know about <topic>, following the schema
and the examples exactly. One idea per entry. Do not invent facts you are not sure
of — set `confidence` honestly and say what you are unsure about in the content.
Return only the JSON.'
WHAT MAKES A GOOD ENTRY
· One idea per entry. Two facts in one entry cannot be approved separately.
· Write what is true about the world, not instructions to a model. Content that reads
as addressed to an assistant is refused by the importer rather than imported.
· No invented specifics. No figures, dates, customer names or contract terms you did
not read somewhere. `confidence: low` is a useful answer; a confident guess is not.
· Say where it came from in `source` — a document, a call, a standard, your own
experience. Knowledge that cannot be traced is hard to approve.
· British English, and keep it short. Somebody reads every one of these.
The `_readme` and `_schema` keys are ignored by the importer. Leave them or delete them.

_schema.contributed_by: REQUIRED. Your name. It travels with every entry and is shown to Owl.
_schema.note: Optional. One line to whoever reviews this batch — what it is and why.
_schema.entries: REQUIRED. A list of entries, each shaped as below. Up to 500 per file.

entry.kind: REQUIRED. One of: glossary | entity | knowledge | research. See `_kinds`.
entry.title: REQUIRED. What the thing is called. Max 120 characters.
entry.description: REQUIRED. One line saying what this entry is. Shown in the review queue.
entry.content: REQUIRED. The knowledge itself, as markdown. Max 20,000 characters.
entry.entity_type: REQUIRED when kind is 'entity'. e.g. protocol, hardware, standard, company.
entry.aliases: Optional. Other names for it, as a list of strings.
entry.tags: Optional. Lowercase keywords, as a list of strings. More are detected on import.
entry.products: Optional. Acme products this relates to, as a list of strings.
entry.source: Optional but wanted. Where this came from.
entry.confidence: Optional. high | medium | low. Defaults to medium.

_kinds.glossary: A term someone might not know. Definition first, then why it matters to Acme.
_kinds.entity: A specific named thing — a protocol, a piece of hardware, a standard, a company.
_kinds.knowledge: How something works, or how it is done. The catch-all for domain understanding.
_kinds.research: A finding, a model, a market or competitor observation. Something learned.

note: Optional one-line note to the reviewer.

entries.title: Holdover
entries.description: What a clock does when it loses its reference, and why the oscillator inside it decides how long that is survivable.
entries.content:
How long a clock can keep accurate time after losing its reference signal — usually GNSS. During holdover the local oscillator free-runs and drifts, so the question is never whether it drifts but how fast.

The oscillator sets the answer. A TCXO drifts out of a microsecond in minutes; an OCXO holds for hours; a rubidium standard holds for days.

**Why it matters commercially:** holdover is what a customer is really buying when they ask about GNSS jamming or antenna access. A site that cannot get a rooftop antenna, or that sits somewhere GNSS is unreliable, is a holdover conversation rather than an antenna one.
entries.source: Standard industry definition plus Acme product positioning

entries.title: SyncE (Synchronous Ethernet)
entries.description: A physical-layer frequency distribution method that complements PTP rather than competing with it.
entries.content:
An ITU-T standard that carries a frequency reference in the Ethernet physical layer, rather than in packets.

Because it is physical-layer, it is not affected by the packet delay variation that degrades PTP under load. It carries **frequency only** — it cannot deliver time of day or phase.

**How it sits with PTP:** the two are usually deployed together. SyncE holds frequency stable while PTP delivers phase and time on top, which is why a network that already runs SyncE is often an easier PTP conversation, not a harder one.

entries.title: Why GNSS antenna access decides the shape of a data centre deal
entries.description: Roof access is a landlord and lease problem before it is a technical one, and it changes what can be sold.
entries.content:
Most data centre timing deployments assume a GNSS antenna on the roof. In colocation that assumption often fails, and for reasons that have nothing to do with engineering: the roof belongs to the landlord, the lease does not grant access, or the facility will not permit new penetrations.

This surfaces late, usually after a technical win, and it is a common reason a deal stalls between agreement and purchase order.

**What to do with it:** ask about antenna access early, in the first technical conversation rather than at design. Where the answer is no, the conversation moves to alternatives — a timing feed from a carrier or neighbouring facility, or a holdover-led design with a better oscillator.

**What I am not sure about:** whether any of the large European colocation providers now offer timing as a facility service. Worth checking before relying on it as an answer.

entries.title: MiFID II RTS 25 timestamp requirements by participant type
entries.description: The regulation sets different accuracy obligations depending on how a firm trades, which changes who has a compliance driver.
entries.content:
RTS 25 does not impose one number on everybody. The obligation scales with activity:

| Activity | Divergence from UTC | Granularity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High-frequency algorithmic trading | 100 microseconds | 1 microsecond |
| Other algorithmic trading | 1 millisecond | 1 millisecond |
| Voice trading | 1 second | 1 second |

**Why it matters for qualification:** a firm's own description of itself is a poor guide to which row it is in, and the row is what decides whether there is a compliance driver at all. A voice desk at one second has no timing problem the regulation creates.

Firms must also be able to *evidence* traceability to UTC, not merely achieve the accuracy — which is a records and monitoring requirement, not only a hardware one.
